𝗠𝗨𝗟𝗧𝗜-𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗜𝗚𝗡 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗦 — 𝗔 𝗖𝗢𝗦𝗧-𝗩𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗘 𝗕𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗞𝗗𝗢𝗪𝗡

Building multi-agent AI systems isn't just about connecting multiple LLMs.

It's about choosing the right architecture to balance cost, performance, scalability, and reliability.

Here are 6 important multi-agent design patterns every AI builder should understand.

𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘’𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗞𝗗𝗢𝗪𝗡:

01 — 𝗦𝗘𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Agents complete tasks one after another in a fixed sequence.

→ Task 1 → Task 2 → Task 3 → Output

→ Best For: Deterministic workflows with clear dependencies.

→ Cost: $

→ Hidden Cost: Slower execution when tasks could run in parallel.

→ Use When: Simplicity and reliability are priorities.

02 — 𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗟 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Multiple agents work on independent tasks simultaneously.

→ Agent A: Handles Task A.

→ Agent B: Handles Task B.

→ Agent C: Handles Task C.

→ Merge: Combines all results.

→ Best For: Reducing latency for independent tasks.

→ Cost: $$

→ Hidden Cost: Higher token usage and infrastructure costs.

→ Avoid When: Tasks depend heavily on each other.

03 — 𝗛𝗜𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗥𝗖𝗛𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

A manager agent delegates tasks to specialized agents.

→ Research Agent: Collects information.

→ Analysis Agent: Evaluates findings.

→ Data Agent: Processes data.

→ Report Agent: Generates reports.

→ Best For: Enterprise-scale workflows.

→ Cost: $$$

→ Hidden Cost: Complex orchestration and higher development effort.

→ Long-Term Value: Reusable sub-agents create leverage across workflows.

04 — 𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗢𝗥–𝗖𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗖 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

One agent generates an output while another reviews and improves it.

→ Generator Agent: Creates the initial output.

→ Critic Agent: Reviews quality and identifies issues.

→ Revision: Improves the generated result.

→ Best For: Content, code, plans, and complex outputs.

→ Cost: $$$

→ Hidden Cost: Multiple inference loops increase latency and cost.

→ Worth It When: Accuracy matters more than speed.

05 — 𝗛𝗨𝗠𝗔𝗡-𝗜𝗡-𝗧𝗛𝗘-𝗟𝗢𝗢𝗣

AI performs tasks while humans review important decisions.

→ AI Agent: Processes the request.

→ Human Review: Checks the result.

→ Action: Executes the approved task.

→ Feedback: Improves future execution.

→ Best For: High-risk decisions and compliance workflows.

→ Cost: $$$

→ Hidden Cost: Manual effort and additional latency.

→ Essential For: Legal, safety, billing, and critical decisions.

06 — 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗢𝗦𝗜𝗧𝗘 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Combines multiple design patterns into one complex workflow.

→ Sequential: Executes dependent tasks.

→ Parallel: Handles independent tasks.

→ Hierarchical: Delegates responsibilities.

→ Generator–Critic: Reviews outputs.

→ Human-in-the-Loop: Adds human approval.

→ Best For: Complex end-to-end automation.

→ Cost: $$$$

→ Hidden Cost: High infrastructure and orchestration overhead.

→ Biggest Mistake: Using it for problems that don't need this complexity.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗖𝗞:

𝗠𝗖𝗣 — 𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗟 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗡𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

Connects AI agents with external tools and data.

→ Tool Access
→ APIs
→ Retrieval
→ Databases
→ External Systems

→ Ecosystem: Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft.

𝗔𝟮𝗔 — 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗖𝗢𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

Enables different AI agents to communicate and collaborate.

→ Agent Messaging
→ Task Delegation
→ Shared Memory
→ Workflow Coordination
→ Capability Discovery

→ Ecosystem: Google, AWS, Microsoft.

More agents don't automatically mean better results.

The right architecture depends on task complexity, budget, execution speed, and reliability requirements.

Start simple. Add orchestration and specialized agents only when they deliver measurable value.

𝗠𝗨𝗟𝗧𝗜-𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗗𝗘𝗦𝗜𝗚𝗡 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡𝗦 — 𝗔 𝗖𝗢𝗦𝗧-𝗩𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗘 𝗕𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗞𝗗𝗢𝗪𝗡

Building multi-agent AI systems isn't just about connecting multiple LLMs.

It's about choosing the right architecture to balance cost, performance, scalability, and reliability.

Here are 6 important multi-agent design patterns every AI builder should understand.

𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘’𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗥𝗘𝗔𝗞𝗗𝗢𝗪𝗡:

01 — 𝗦𝗘𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗡𝗧𝗜𝗔𝗟 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Agents complete tasks one after another in a fixed sequence.

→ Task 1 → Task 2 → Task 3 → Output

→ Best For: Deterministic workflows with clear dependencies.

→ Cost: $

→ Hidden Cost: Slower execution when tasks could run in parallel.

→ Use When: Simplicity and reliability are priorities.

02 — 𝗣𝗔𝗥𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗟 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Multiple agents work on independent tasks simultaneously.

→ Agent A: Handles Task A.

→ Agent B: Handles Task B.

→ Agent C: Handles Task C.

→ Merge: Combines all results.

→ Best For: Reducing latency for independent tasks.

→ Cost: $$

→ Hidden Cost: Higher token usage and infrastructure costs.

→ Avoid When: Tasks depend heavily on each other.

03 — 𝗛𝗜𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗥𝗖𝗛𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

A manager agent delegates tasks to specialized agents.

→ Research Agent: Collects information.

→ Analysis Agent: Evaluates findings.

→ Data Agent: Processes data.

→ Report Agent: Generates reports.

→ Best For: Enterprise-scale workflows.

→ Cost: $$$

→ Hidden Cost: Complex orchestration and higher development effort.

→ Long-Term Value: Reusable sub-agents create leverage across workflows.

04 — 𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗢𝗥–𝗖𝗥𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗖 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

One agent generates an output while another reviews and improves it.

→ Generator Agent: Creates the initial output.

→ Critic Agent: Reviews quality and identifies issues.

→ Revision: Improves the generated result.

→ Best For: Content, code, plans, and complex outputs.

→ Cost: $$$

→ Hidden Cost: Multiple inference loops increase latency and cost.

→ Worth It When: Accuracy matters more than speed.

05 — 𝗛𝗨𝗠𝗔𝗡-𝗜𝗡-𝗧𝗛𝗘-𝗟𝗢𝗢𝗣

AI performs tasks while humans review important decisions.

→ AI Agent: Processes the request.

→ Human Review: Checks the result.

→ Action: Executes the approved task.

→ Feedback: Improves future execution.

→ Best For: High-risk decisions and compliance workflows.

→ Cost: $$$

→ Hidden Cost: Manual effort and additional latency.

→ Essential For: Legal, safety, billing, and critical decisions.

06 — 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗢𝗦𝗜𝗧𝗘 𝗣𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗡

Combines multiple design patterns into one complex workflow.

→ Sequential: Executes dependent tasks.

→ Parallel: Handles independent tasks.

→ Hierarchical: Delegates responsibilities.

→ Generator–Critic: Reviews outputs.

→ Human-in-the-Loop: Adds human approval.

→ Best For: Complex end-to-end automation.

→ Cost: $$$$

→ Hidden Cost: High infrastructure and orchestration overhead.

→ Biggest Mistake: Using it for problems that don't need this complexity.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗗𝗨𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗦𝗧𝗔𝗖𝗞:

𝗠𝗖𝗣 — 𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗟 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗡𝗘𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗩𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

Connects AI agents with external tools and data.

→ Tool Access
→ APIs
→ Retrieval
→ Databases
→ External Systems

→ Ecosystem: Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft.

𝗔𝟮𝗔 — 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗖𝗢𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

Enables different AI agents to communicate and collaborate.

→ Agent Messaging
→ Task Delegation
→ Shared Memory
→ Workflow Coordination
→ Capability Discovery

→ Ecosystem: Google, AWS, Microsoft.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗞𝗘𝗬 𝗟𝗘𝗦𝗦𝗢𝗡:

More agents don't automatically mean better results.

The right architecture depends on task complexity, budget, execution speed, and reliability requirements.

Start simple. Add orchestration and specialized agents only when they deliver measurable value.
